summary.text: A finite modular computation shows that 283411 is prime, that \(28341^{28341}\equiv1\pmod{283411^2}\), and that \(28341^d\not\equiv1\pmod{283411}\) for every proper divisor \(d\mid28341\). Evaluating \(\prod_{d\mid n}\Phi_d(X)=X^n-1\) at \(n=28341\), and using \(\Phi_d(n)\mid n^d-1\), makes the product of all proper-divisor factors coprime to 283411, so the full square factor must divide the remaining top cyclotomic value.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
n=28341,\qquad p=283411,
\]
and let \(\Phi_m(X)\) denote the \(m\)-th cyclotomic polynomial. We prove that
\[
p^2\mid \Phi_n(n).
\]
Since the sequence term is defined as the nonnegative absolute value of this integer, this will give \(p^2\mid a(n)\).

We first record the numerical facts that will be used.

### 1. Factorizations and primality

The relevant factorizations are
\[
28341=3^2\cdot 47\cdot 67
\]
and
\[
p-1=283410=2\cdot 3^2\cdot 5\cdot 47\cdot 67.
\]
The numbers \(47\) and \(67\) are prime: trial division by primes not exceeding their square roots, namely \(2,3,5\) for \(47\), and \(2,3,5,7\) for \(67\), suffices.

We also need that \(p=283411\) is prime. Here is a compact Lucas primality certificate. Repeated squaring modulo \(p\) gives
\[
2^{283410}\equiv 1\pmod p,
\]
and, for the distinct prime divisors \(q=2,3,5,47,67\) of \(p-1\), it gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
q&2^{(p-1)/q}\pmod p\\ \hline
2&283410\\
3&153836\\
5&174613\\
47&147198\\
67&236184.
\end{array}
\]
None of the entries in the second column is congruent to \(1\) modulo \(p\). More explicitly, the following Bézout identities show that each entry minus \(1\) is relatively prime to \(p\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
141705(283410-1)-141704(283411)&=1,\\
43191(153836-1)-23444(283411)&=1,\\
80838(174613-1)-49805(283411)&=1,\\
79994(147198-1)-41547(283411)&=1,\\
19773(236184-1)-16478(283411)&=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Lucas's primality criterion says that if an integer \(N>1\) has an integer \(b\) such that
\[
b^{N-1}\equiv1\pmod N
\]
and
\[
\gcd\bigl(b^{(N-1)/q}-1,N\bigr)=1
\]
for every prime divisor \(q\) of \(N-1\), then \(N\) is prime. Applying this with \(N=p\) and \(b=2\) proves that \(p=283411\) is prime.

### 2. The square divisibility of \(n^n-1\)

We next verify
\[
p^2\mid n^n-1.
\]
The modulus is
\[
p^2=283411^2=80321794921.
\]
For completeness, this congruence can be checked by the following square-and-multiply computation. Put \(M=80321794921\). Successive squaring of \(n=28341\) modulo \(M\) gives, for exponents \(2^0,2^1,\ldots,2^{14}\), the residues
\[
\begin{array}{c|r}
j&28341^{2^j}\pmod M\\ \hline
0&28341\\
1&803212281\\
2&10305286175\\
3&56856623504\\
4&11119560660\\
5&34823658856\\
6&7305860158\\
7&72720565854\\
8&77339958728\\
9&48530202121\\
10&18484540212\\
11&77970117019\\
12&39630026099\\
13&23437256541\\
14&8780247748.
\end{array}
\]
Each row is obtained by squaring the preceding residue and reducing modulo \(M\). The binary decomposition
\[
28341=2^{14}+2^{13}+2^{11}+2^{10}+2^9+2^7+2^5+2^4+2^2+2^0
\]
therefore allows us to multiply just the corresponding rows. Taking them in increasing order of the exponent, the successive accumulated residues are
\[
\begin{array}{c|r}
\text{newly included }2^j&\text{accumulated residue modulo }M\\ \hline
2^0&28341\\
2^2&12069152919\\
2^4&58902886234\\
2^5&3524814247\\
2^7&59346352675\\
2^9&71235197045\\
2^{10}&8309007975\\
2^{11}&79405617822\\
2^{13}&20736622302\\
2^{14}&1.
\end{array}
\]
Thus
\[
28341^{28341}\equiv1\pmod{80321794921},
\]
which is exactly
\[
p^2\mid n^n-1. \tag{1}
\]

### 3. The order calculation modulo \(p\)

We now show that \(p\) does not divide \(n^d-1\) for any proper positive divisor \(d\) of \(n\).

From \(n=3^2\cdot47\cdot67\), all positive divisors are obtained by choosing a power \(3^e\) with \(e=0,1,2\), optionally multiplying by \(47\), and optionally multiplying by \(67\). Removing \(n\) itself, the proper positive divisors are therefore precisely
\[
1,3,9,47,67,141,201,423,603,3149,9447.
\]
Repeated squaring modulo \(p=283411\) gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|r}
j&28341^{2^j}\pmod p\\ \hline
0&28341\\
1&25507\\
2&178804\\
3&125739\\
4&213486\\
5&99053\\
6&91400\\
7&137364\\
8&214349\\
9&36125\\
10&191381\\
11&66576\\
12&99147\\
13&17074\\
14&174968.
\end{array}
\]
Using the binary expansion of each proper divisor and multiplying the corresponding entries yields
\[
\begin{array}{c|r}
d&28341^d\pmod{283411}\\ \hline
1&28341\\
3&195837\\
9&242496\\
47&279371\\
67&113273\\
141&272904\\
201&172838\\
423&196258\\
603&168687\\
3149&168564\\
9447&153836.
\end{array}
\]
Every displayed residue differs from \(1\). Consequently,
\[
p\nmid n^d-1
\quad\text{for every proper positive divisor }d\text{ of }n. \tag{2}
\]
Equivalently, together with \(n^n\equiv1\pmod p\), this says that the multiplicative order of \(n\) modulo \(p\) is exactly \(n\), although only the nondivisibility statement (2) will be needed.

### 4. Isolating the top cyclotomic factor

The standard cyclotomic factorization is
\[
X^m-1=\prod_{d\mid m}\Phi_d(X)
\]
for every positive integer \(m\). Applying it with \(m=n\) and then evaluating at \(X=n\) gives
\[
n^n-1=\prod_{d\mid n}\Phi_d(n).
\]
Separate the factor corresponding to the divisor \(d=n\). If
\[
B=\prod_{\substack{d\mid n\\d<n}}\Phi_d(n),
\]
then
\[
\Phi_n(n)B=n^n-1. \tag{3}
\]

We claim that \(p\nmid B\). For every positive divisor \(d\) of \(n\), the cyclotomic factorization with exponent \(d\) shows that \(\Phi_d(X)\) is an integer-polynomial divisor of \(X^d-1\). Evaluating at \(X=n\), we obtain the integer divisibility
\[
\Phi_d(n)\mid n^d-1. \tag{4}
\]
Suppose that \(d<n\) divides \(n\) and that \(p\mid\Phi_d(n)\). By (4), transitivity of divisibility would imply
\[
p\mid n^d-1,
\]
contrary to (2). Thus
\[
p\nmid\Phi_d(n)
\quad\text{for every proper divisor }d\text{ of }n. \tag{5}
\]

Because \(p\) is prime, if it divided the finite product \(B\), Euclid's lemma would force it to divide one of the factors in that product. This contradicts (5), so indeed
\[
p\nmid B.
\]
Since \(p\) is prime, this is equivalent to \(\gcd(p,B)=1\), and hence also
\[
\gcd(p^2,B)=1. \tag{6}
\]
(The possible signs of the integer cyclotomic values do not affect any of these divisibility or gcd statements.)

Finally, (1) and (3) show that
\[
p^2\mid \Phi_n(n)B.
\]
By (6), \(p^2\) is relatively prime to \(B\). Euclid's lemma in its coprime form—if \(r\mid xy\) and \(\gcd(r,y)=1\), then \(r\mid x\)—therefore yields
\[
p^2\mid\Phi_n(n).
\]

By definition,
\[
a(28341)=\left|\Phi_{28341}(28341)\right|.
\]
If a positive integer divides an integer, it also divides its absolute value. Therefore
\[
283411^2\mid a(28341),
\]
as required.
